sections.section_title: Case Presentation and Initial Clinical Assessment
sections.description: This section presents the patient's initial clinical presentation following a dog bite, including early symptoms, physical examination findings, and initial laboratory abnormalities. It establishes the clinical context of sepsis and multiorgan dysfunction, introduces Capnocytophaga canimorsus as the causative pathogen, and covers the initial diagnostic approach and management decisions made upon admission.
subtopics: Patient history and timeline: dog bite, missed antibiotic prophylaxis, and symptom progression
Clinical presentation on admission: septic syndrome, mottled extremities, hypoglycemia
Initial laboratory profile: pancytopenia, AKI, coagulopathy, lactic acidosis
Capnocytophaga canimorsus: microbiology, transmission, and clinical manifestations
Initial differential diagnosis: sepsis, DIC, necrotizing fasciitis, hematologic emergencies
Empiric antibiotic selection targeting dog-associated pathogens
Clinical suspicion of C. canimorsus and confirmatory blood cultures

sections.section_title: Disease Evolution and Recognition of Thrombotic Microangiopathy
sections.description: This section describes how the patient's clinical course evolved from initial septic presentation to the emergence of features consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy. It highlights the clinical challenge of identifying TMA when it develops in the context of resolving sepsis and DIC, and explains the key laboratory features that prompted further diagnostic workup.
subtopics: Clinical trajectory in ICU: anuria, dialysis dependence, septic cardiomyopathy
Resolution of sepsis parameters and improvement in inflammatory markers
Emergence of isolated hemolysis: sudden hemoglobin drop, rising LDH, undetectable haptoglobin
Peripheral blood smear findings: schistocytes (15-20%) indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
False-positive direct antiglobulin test and initial misdiagnosis of autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Differentiating TMA from ongoing DIC: timing, laboratory features, clinical context
Clinical recognition: when to suspect superimposed TMA in recovering sepsis

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Diagnostic Workup for Thrombotic Microangiopathy
sections.description: This section provides a systematic approach to the differential diagnosis of thrombotic microangiopathy, focusing on the key entities: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), Shiga toxin-producing E. coli HUS (STEC-HUS), and complement-mediated HUS (CM-HUS). It explains the diagnostic tests used, their interpretation, and how each diagnosis was ruled in or out.
subtopics: Classification of TMA syndromes and clinical overlap
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: PLASMIC score, ADAMTS13 activity, and diagnostic criteria
STEC-HUS: clinical features, prodromal diarrhea, and Shiga toxin PCR testing
Complement-mediated HUS: diagnostic criteria and exclusions
Kidney biopsy findings in TMA: acute tubular necrosis, ischaemic glomeruli, fibrin thrombi
Interpretation of complement studies: C3/C4 levels, alternative pathway activity (AH50)
Stepwise diagnostic algorithm for TMA in adults

sections.description: This section explains the underlying pathophysiology of complement-mediated HUS, including the role of alternative complement pathway dysregulation, genetic predisposition, and triggering events. It specifically addresses how C. canimorsus infection may trigger CM-HUS and the mechanism by which complement dysregulation leads to thrombotic microangiopathy.
subtopics: Alternative complement pathway: physiology, regulation, and terminal pathway activation
Complement regulatory proteins: Factor H, Factor I, Factor B, and membrane cofactor protein (CD46)
Genetic variants in CM-HUS: penetrance and the 'second hit' hypothesis
Role of infectious triggers in precipitating CM-HUS
Mechanism of endothelial injury and microthrombus formation
C. canimorsus and complement interaction: serum susceptibility and capsule expression
CM-HUS without identifiable genetic variants: infection-triggered disease

sections.description: This section covers the therapeutic approach to CM-HUS, including the rationale for plasma exchange as bridging therapy and the definitive treatment with complement inhibition using eculizumab. It addresses the clinical dilemma of initiating complement blockade relative to active infection, the importance of vaccination and antimicrobial prophylaxis, and the patient's clinical outcome and prognosis.
subtopics: Plasma exchange: role as bridging therapy and limitations in CM-HUS
Eculizumab: mechanism of action targeting C5, induction and maintenance dosing
Therapeutic dilemma: complement blockade and risk of uncontrolled infection
Meningococcal vaccination and antimicrobial prophylaxis requirements
Timing of eculizumab initiation: balancing infection risk with renal recovery
Clinical response: return of diuresis, hematological remission, partial renal recovery
Prognostic factors in CM-HUS: time to treatment and renal outcome
Long-term management: duration of complement blockade and monitoring for relapse
